subject: Medicine
summary: Gastritis is inflammation of the gastric mucosa that can be acute or chronic. In East Africa, infections, medications, and nutritional factors dominate. Clinical reasoning focuses on history, bedside signs, and pragmatic investigations.

sections.p: Gastritis is mucosal inflammation of the stomach lining. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by simple tests when available. In low‑resource settings, a focused history and bedside examination guide management.
b: Acute: sudden epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, possible haematemesis or melena
Chronic: dull epigastric discomfort, early satiety, weight loss

Is thrombocytopenia present? May indicate portal hypertension or bone marrow suppression

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical features and endoscopic findings. In practice, we use a simple three‑tier system: mild, moderate, severe.
b: Mild: pain only, no bleeding, normal vitals
Moderate: pain with vomiting, mild tachycardia, possible occult blood
Severe: haematemesis, melena, hypotension, tachycardia, or shock

t.b: Assess haemodynamic stability; hypotension or tachycardia indicates severe bleeding

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected acute gastritis?
faq.a: Stop any offending drugs, give a proton pump inhibitor, and assess haemodynamic stability.

faq.q: Why is a proton pump inhibitor preferred over H2 blockers in acute gastritis?
faq.a: PPIs provide stronger acid suppression and faster symptom relief, reducing bleeding risk.

faq.q: How do you treat H. pylori in a setting without culture facilities?
faq.a: Use a standard triple therapy regimen (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin) if local resistance is low, otherwise use bismuth quadruple therapy.

exam: What is the most likely cause of acute epigastric pain with haematemesis in a patient on NSAIDs? — NSAID‑induced erosive gastritis; explain pathophysiology and immediate management steps.

A patient presents with dull epigastric discomfort, early satiety, and weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis and first investigation? — Chronic gastritis, likely H. pylori; first test is rapid urease test.
During a ward round you find a patient with melena and hypotension. What is the next step? — Immediate resuscitation with IV fluids, blood transfusion if needed, and urgent endoscopy if available.
Why is tranexamic acid contraindicated in a patient with a history of thromboembolism? — It stabilises clots and increases risk of thrombosis.
A patient on chronic antipsychotics develops epigastric pain. Which drug class should be avoided and why? — NSAIDs/aspirin; they increase gastric mucosal damage.
Explain how autoimmune gastritis leads to pernicious anaemia. — Loss of parietal cells → achlorhydria → impaired B12 absorption → macrocytic anaemia.

In a resource‑limited setting, how would you differentiate gastritis from peptic ulcer disease based on bedside findings? — Look for pain relief with food (PUD) vs pain with NSAIDs/alcohol (gastritis).

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and a systematic abdominal exam allow rapid risk stratification of gastritis in low‑resource settings. Use open‑ended questions, then targeted probes, and examine for signs of bleeding, irritation and systemic illness.
b: Onset, duration and pattern of epigastric pain (sudden vs gradual, relation to meals, nocturnal).
Associated symptoms: nausea, vomiting (frequency, presence of coffee‑ground material), melena, haematemesis, early satiety, weight loss.
Medication history: NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelet agents, steroids, antiretrovirals, psychotropics, herbal remedies (e.g., Kigelia).
Infection risk: recent malaria, HIV status, TB exposure, recent antibiotics.
Alcohol and tobacco use, dietary irritants, stressors (critical illness, burns).
Pregnancy status, age extremes, comorbid renal or liver disease.

t.b: Look for abdominal distension, visible vomiting, pallor or jaundice; cannot diagnose gastritis but may suggest bleeding or chronic disease.
Listen for bowel sounds; hyperactive sounds may accompany irritation, absent sounds suggest ileus; does not differentiate gastritis from ulcer.
Gentle pressure over the epigastrium; pain reproducible suggests mucosal irritation; guarding or rigidity points to perforation, not simple gastritis.
Assess for gastric distension; tympanic note may indicate retained gastric contents in acute gastritis; cannot confirm inflammation.
Negative in gastritis; a positive sign suggests hepatobiliary disease, helping exclude mimics.

sections.p: Prioritise tests that change immediate management and are affordable. When a test is unavailable, use clinical algorithms or substitute bedside alternatives.

sections.p: Combine history, exam and available investigations to classify gastritis for treatment and referral decisions.
b: Acute gastritis – sudden epigastric pain, vomiting, possible haematemesis; usually triggered by NSAIDs, alcohol, infection; endoscopic erythema if visualised.
Chronic gastritis – dull epigastric discomfort, early satiety, weight loss; often H. pylori‑related or autoimmune; may show atrophic mucosa.

Severity grading (clinical): Mild – pain only, vitals stable, no bleeding; Moderate – vomiting, tachycardia > 100 bpm, occult blood; Severe – haematemesis, melena, SBP < 90 mmHg, tachycardia > 120 bpm, shock.
Staging (endoscopic when possible): Non‑erosive gastritis, erosive gastritis, ulcerated gastritis; each higher stage predicts bleeding risk.
Complication flags: perforation (rigid abdomen, free air on X‑ray), massive bleeding (requiring transfusion), gastric outlet obstruction (persistent vomiting, palpable mass).

sections.p: Several diseases mimic gastritis clinically or endoscopically; key discriminators are distribution, associated labs and response to therapy.

t.b: Pain often improves with food or antacids; endoscopy shows discrete ulcer crater; positive occult blood common. Differentiate by ulcer base on endoscopy.
Heartburn and regurgitation predominate; symptoms worsen lying down; endoscopy shows oesophagitis, not gastric mucosal inflammation.
Epigastric pain radiates to back, associated with elevated amylase/lipase; bedside exam may show guarding; labs differentiate.
Weight loss, early satiety, palpable mass, anemia; endoscopy shows mass lesion, not diffuse erythema; biopsy confirms.
Rare; history of TB, systemic symptoms; endoscopy may show ulcerated lesions with caseating granulomas; acid‑fast stain needed.

sections.p: Treat acute gastritis by stabilising the patient, eradicating infection if present, and protecting the mucosa. Escalate to endoscopy or surgery if bleeding persists or complications develop.
b: 1. Resuscitate: IV fluids, monitor vitals, give oxygen if needed.
2. Stop offending agents: NSAIDs, antimalarials, antiretrovirals, alcohol, herbal remedies.
3. Start mucosal protection: proton‑pump inhibitor (e.g., omeprazole) or H2‑blocker (famotidine) for at least 7–14 days.
4. Eradicate H. pylori if suspected: triple therapy (PPI, amoxicillin, clarithromycin) or bismuth‑based regimen if resistance high.
5. Treat underlying causes: manage HIV with ART, treat TB with ATT, correct malnutrition, stop stressors.
6. Monitor: repeat haemoglobin, repeat vitals, watch for melena, hematemesis, hypotension.
7. Escalate: urgent endoscopy if ongoing bleeding, haemodynamic instability, or suspicion of ulcer perforation.
8. Refer: surgical consultation for perforation or uncontrolled bleeding; transplant team if severe liver failure; infectious disease for complex TB/HIV cases.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Mucosal protectants and antibiotics have specific adverse effects and interactions that must be recognised and managed.
b: 1. PPIs: risk of hypomagnesemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, Clostridioides difficile infection; monitor electrolytes and B12 in long‑term users.
2. H2‑blockers: tachyphylaxis, constipation; switch to PPI if ineffective.
3. Clarithromycin: QT prolongation, drug interactions with protease inhibitors; avoid in patients on ritonavir or cobicistat.
4. Amoxicillin: rash, GI upset; monitor for allergic reaction.
5. Metronidazole: neurotoxicity, disulfiram‑like reaction with alcohol; counsel patient to avoid alcohol.
6. Antiretrovirals: CYP3A4 induction or inhibition with PPIs; adjust doses or choose alternative antacid.
7. NSAIDs: avoid in active gastritis; if needed, co‑prescribe PPI and use lowest effective dose.

sections.p: Early recognition of complications prevents morbidity and mortality. Escalation is required when signs of severe disease or failure of medical therapy appear.
b: 1. Active upper GI bleeding: persistent haematemesis, melena, tachycardia >100 bpm, SBP <90 mmHg, or drop in haemoglobin >2 g/dL within 24 h – urgent endoscopy and transfusion.
2. Perforation: sudden severe epigastric pain, rigidity, rebound tenderness, free air on X‑ray – emergency surgery.
3. Gastric outlet obstruction: vomiting of undigested food, weight loss, dehydration – endoscopic dilation or surgical bypass if refractory.
4. Severe gastritis with shock: hypotension, oliguria, altered mental status – ICU admission, vasopressors, broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected.
5. Recurrent bleeding after initial control: repeat endoscopy, consider angiographic embolisation or surgery.

sections.p: These conditions alter presentation, investigation, or treatment of gastritis and must be considered in every patient.
b: 1. HIV: increases risk of H. pylori, opportunistic infections, drug interactions with ART; screen for CD4 and viral load.
2. TB: can cause gastric ulceration, may require ATT which interacts with PPIs; monitor for hepatotoxicity.
3. Malnutrition: reduces mucosal healing, increases bleeding risk; provide protein‑rich diet and vitamin supplementation.
4. Pregnancy: avoid high‑dose PPIs and clarithromycin; use amoxicillin + metronidazole after first trimester; use H2‑blocker for symptom control.
5. Diabetes: gastroparesis may mimic gastritis; monitor blood glucose as steroids or PPIs can raise glucose.
6. Herbal remedies (e.g., Kigelia, miso): may contain alkaloids that irritate mucosa; ask about all supplements.
7. Alcohol: chronic use causes erosive gastritis; counsel abstinence and provide NPO if bleeding.
8. Renal or liver failure: dose adjust PPIs, avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics, monitor for hepatic encephalopathy if using antiretrovirals.
9. Age extremes: children have different drug tolerances; elderly have higher bleeding risk and polypharmacy.

sections.p: Tailored management is essential for vulnerable populations to optimise outcomes and minimise harm.
b: 1. Children: use age‑appropriate formulations of PPIs; avoid NSAIDs; consider H. pylori testing if recurrent pain.
2. Pregnancy: use H2‑blocker or low‑dose PPI; treat H. pylori with amoxicillin + metronidazole after first trimester; avoid tetracyclines.
3. Elderly: monitor for drug interactions, renal clearance; use lowest effective dose of PPIs; watch for confusion or falls from hypomagnesemia.
4. People with HIV: monitor drug interactions with ART, screen for opportunistic infections, consider prophylactic PPIs only if indicated.
5. Low‑resource settings: rely on stool occult blood, basic metabolic panel, and bedside assessment; use affordable empiric therapy; refer only if bleeding or perforation suspected.

sections.p: Sample questions covering bedside, investigations, management, complications and special factors.

t.a: A 45‑year‑old man on long‑term ibuprofen presents with haematemesis. What is the first step in management?
t.b: Resuscitate with IV fluids, stop ibuprofen, start a PPI, and arrange urgent endoscopy if bleeding persists.

t.a: A patient with chronic gastritis has a serum gastrin of 150 pg/mL and normal pH. What does this suggest?
t.b: Autoimmune gastritis with loss of negative feedback; consider pernicious anaemia.

t.a: Which drug interaction should be avoided when treating H. pylori in a patient on ritonavir?
t.b: Clarithromycin – it prolongs QT and is metabolised by CYP3A4, leading to toxicity.

t.a: A pregnant woman in her second trimester has epigastric pain and melena. What is the safest H. pylori regimen?
t.b: Amoxicillin plus metronidazole; avoid clarithromycin and tetracyclines.

t.a: A 70‑year‑old woman with known cirrhosis develops sudden epigastric pain and hypotension. What is the most likely compli
t.b: Gastric ulcer perforation – urgent surgical consultation.

t.a: In a resource‑limited setting, which test is most useful to confirm H. pylori?
t.b: Stool antigen test or rapid urease test if endoscopy unavailable.

t.a: What is the threshold for severe gastritis on tachycardia?
t.b: Tachycardia >100 bpm with hypotension or haemoglobin drop >2 g/dL.

t.a: A child presents with vomiting and epigastric pain. Which drug class should be avoided?
t.b: NSAIDs – they increase risk of erosive gastritis in children.

facts: Acute gastritis severity: mild pain only; moderate vomiting, tachycardia >100 bpm; severe haematemesis, melena, SBP <90 mmHg or HR >120 bpm
H. pylori gastritis: most common chronic gastritis in East Africa
Autoimmune gastritis: gastrin >100 pg/mL, anti‑parietal cell antibodies present
Zollinger‑Ellison syndrome: gastrin >1000 pg/mL in normal pH
Pregnancy H. pylori therapy: amoxicillin + metronidazole after first trimester
Herbal preparations (e.g., Kigelia) can cause gastritis; avoid high‑dose antimalarials
Stool occult blood: positive indicates upper GI bleeding; negative does not exclude gastritis

vivas.q: What is the most likely cause of acute epigastric pain with haematemesis in a patient on NSAIDs?
vivas.a: NSAID‑induced erosive gastritis; NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reducing mucosal protection.

vivas.q: A patient presents with dull epigastric discomfort, early satiety, and weight loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
vivas.a: Chronic gastritis, likely H. pylori‑related with NSAID contribution; consider autoimmune gastritis if anaemia present.

vivas.q: During a ward round you find a patient with melena and hypotension. What is the next step?
vivas.a: Stabilise with IV fluids, give a proton pump inhibitor, and arrange urgent endoscopy for source control.

vivas.q: Why is tranexamic acid contraindicated in a patient with a history of thromboembolism?
vivas.a: It promotes clot stability and can precipitate new thrombotic events.

vivas.q: A patient on chronic antipsychotics develops epigastric pain. Which drug class should be avoided and why?
vivas.a: Antipsychotics with anticholinergic properties (e.g., clozapine) worsen gastric motility and increase ulcer risk.

vivas.q: Explain how autoimmune gastritis leads to pernicious anaemia.
vivas.a: Loss of parietal cells reduces intrinsic factor, impairing B12 absorption, causing macrocytic anaemia.

vivas.q: In a resource‑limited setting, how would you differentiate gastritis from peptic ulcer disease?
vivas.a: Use bedside signs: ulcer pain often radiates to back, may have visible peristaltic waves; gastritis pain is diffuse. Endoscopy confirms.

vivas.q: What is the deepest layer of the gastric wall involved in true gastritis?
vivas.a: The mucosa, including the epithelium, lamina propria, and muscularis mucosae.

vivas.q: Which form of chronic gastritis specifically involves the fundus and body of the stomach and is primarily autoimmune-mediated?
Describe the histological features of acute gastritis.
vivas.a: Neutrophilic infiltration of the mucosa, erosions, and possible ulceration.

vivas.q: Describe the histological features of chronic gastritis.
vivas.a: Lymphoid aggregates, plasmacytosis, atrophy of glands, intestinal metaplasia.

vivas.q: Differentiate between Type A and Type B chronic gastritis based on distribution and etiology.
vivas.a: Type A: autoimmune, body/fundus; Type B: H. pylori, antrum.

vivas.q: Describe the role of prostaglandins in the pathogenesis of gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.
vivas.a: Prostaglandins stimulate mucus and bicarbonate, maintain mucosal blood flow; NSAIDs inhibit them, leading to mucosal injury.

vivas.q: Differentiate H. pylori‑associated chronic gastritis and autoimmune gastritis in terms of location of inflammation, acid secretion, gastrin levels, associated antibodies, and risk of pernicious anaemia.
vivas.a: H. pylori: antrum, normal acid, gastrin normal, no antibodies, low anaemia risk; autoimmune: body/fundus, hypochlorhydria, gastrin >100 pg/mL, anti‑parietal cell antibodies, high anaemia risk.

mcqs.q: A 45‑year‑old woman with chronic epigastric pain and early satiety has a gastric biopsy showing lymphoid aggregates and intestinal metaplasia. Which antibody is most likely present?
mcqs.e: Autoimmune gastritis shows anti‑parietal cell antibodies.

mcqs.q: Which drug is contraindicated in pregnancy for H. pylori eradication?
A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops gastritis. Which PPI interaction should be monitored?
Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of acute gastritis in East Africa?
mcqs.e: Beta‑blockers are not a common cause.

mcqs.q: A 60‑year‑old man with chronic NSAID use has a gastritis score of 3. What does this indicate?

cases.v: A 52‑year‑old male presents with dull epigastric pain, early satiety, weight loss, and mild anemia. He is a chronic NSAID user. Vitals: HR 90, BP 110/70. Labs: CBC shows Hb 11.5 g/dL, MCV 105 fL. Stool occult blood negative.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Chronic gastritis, likely H. pylori‑related with NSAID contribution; consider autoimmune gastritis due to macrocytosis.

qs.q: Which investigation would you order next?
qs.a: Urea breath test or stool antigen for H. pylori; if unavailable, serology. Also consider endoscopy if alarm features.

qs.q: What is the first step in management?
qs.a: Stop NSAIDs, start a proton pump inhibitor, and treat H. pylori if confirmed.

mistakes: Assuming all haematemesis in NSAID users is due to ulcers; gastritis can also bleed
Ignoring the need for urgent endoscopy in any upper GI bleed
Treating H. pylori with clarithromycin in pregnancy
Overlooking macrocytic anaemia as a sign of autoimmune gastritis
Using high‑dose PPIs prophylactically in all HIV patients on protease inhibitors
Misreading stool occult blood as negative when bleeding is intermittent
Failing to differentiate gastritis from peptic ulcer disease based on pain location
Assuming all chronic gastritis is H. pylori‑related without considering autoimmune causes
